title: NSMP versus p53-mutated endometrial carcinomas; a retrospective data analysis of the patient records from the Department of Gynecology and Gynecologic Oncology at the University Hospital Bonn (2020–2025) with regard to the tumor stage at initial diagnosis, as well as the occurrence of the symptom of postmenopausal/atypical bleeding.
summary:
Endometrial carcinoma is the fifth most common malignancy in women, with approximately 11,000 new cases diagnosed each year. In Germany, the mean age at diagnosis is 68 years. The leading symptom of endometrial carcinoma is atypical bleeding, particularly postmenopausal bleeding. In principle, endometrial carcinoma can be divided into two groups according to the dualistic model.

Type I carcinomas mainly include endometrioid and mucinous endometrial carcinomas. With a proportion of 70–80%, they represent the largest group. An important distinction from type II carcinomas is their estrogen dependence. Type II carcinomas, which account for around 10% and thus represent the significantly smaller group, mainly include serous tumors. In this category, clear cell endometrial carcinomas and carcinosarcomas are particularly notable. Mixed carcinomas are defined as tumors in which two or more histological subtypes are present.

However, genomic or molecular classification is becoming increasingly important. Four molecular subtypes are distinguished: POLE-mutant, MMR-deficient, non-specific molecular profile (NSMP), and p53-abnormal. Precise determination of the mutation type is of crucial importance with regard to therapy and prognosis. While the first three of the above-mentioned mutation types generally show a good to intermediate prognosis, p53-mutated endometrial carcinomas are notable for their often poor prognosis and advanced tumor stage at initial diagnosis.

The aim of this dissertation is to investigate to what extent the symptom of postmenopausal or atypical bleeding in p53-mutated endometrial carcinomas represents a symptom that occurs only in advanced tumor stages. For this purpose, the anonymized data of patients diagnosed with endometrial carcinoma who were treated at the Department of Gynecology and Gynecologic Oncology at the University Hospital Bonn between 2020 and 2025 will be analyzed in a retrospective study. Of central relevance are the clinical symptoms, the molecular subtype, and the tumor stage at the time of initial diagnosis. This analysis aims to determine whether there is a significant, prognostically relevant difference between NSMP endometrial carcinomas and p53-mutated endometrial carcinomas.

The treatment of endometrial carcinoma is generally stage-dependent; however, the primary therapy consists of surgical removal of the uterus and both adnexa, with additional removal of the pelvic and paraaortic lymph nodes depending on the individual risk profile. Radiotherapy as well as chemotherapy are important adjuvant treatment options.

interventions.name: This is a retrospective data analysis of patient data generated in routine clinical practice from patients who were treated between 2020 and 2025 at the Department of Gynecology and Gynecologic Oncology at the University Hospital Bonn.
